claims.text: A commit stores a complete snapshot of the tracked files, not the lines that differ from the previous commit; the commit object names that snapshot with a `tree` line.
claims.source_hint: git-commit documentation, DESCRIPTION (records a snapshot of the current contents of the index); gitglossary, entries 'commit' and 'tree-ish'

claims.text: A commit object holds, in this order, a tree line, zero or more parent lines, an author line with a time, a committer line with a time, a blank line, and the message; `git cat-file -p HEAD` prints it in that raw form.
claims.source_hint: git-cat-file documentation, -p option; gitformat-commit / 'Git Internals - Git Objects' commit object format

claims.text: The parent line of a commit holds the id of the commit it was made from. History is read by starting at the current commit and following parent links backwards until a commit has no parent.
claims.source_hint: gitglossary, entries 'parent' and 'commit'; git-log documentation, DESCRIPTION (lists commits reachable by following parent links)

claims.text: A commit may name more than one parent, and several commits may name the same parent, so the set of commits forms a directed graph rather than a line.
claims.source_hint: gitglossary, entries 'DAG', 'parent', 'merge'; git-log documentation, --graph

claims.text: A change passes through three places: the working directory (working tree), the staging area written by `git add`, and the repository written by `git commit`. `git commit` records what the staging area holds, not what is on disk.
claims.source_hint: git-add documentation, DESCRIPTION; git-commit documentation, DESCRIPTION and 'the current contents of the index'; gitglossary 'working tree'

claims.text: `git status --short` prints two status columns per file: the left one for the staging area, the right one for the working directory. ` M` means modified on disk only; `M ` means the modification has been staged.
claims.source_hint: git-status documentation, 'Short Format': XY where X is the index status and Y the work tree status

claims.text: `git add <file>` copies the file's content as it stands at that moment into the staging area; editing the file afterwards leaves the staged copy unchanged, which `git status --short` shows by marking both columns.
claims.source_hint: git-add documentation, DESCRIPTION ('It only adds the content of the specified file(s) at the time the add command is run'); git-status documentation, Short Format

claims.text: A commit's id is computed from the commit object's own content, which includes the tree id, the parent id, the author and committer lines with their times, and the message; changing any of them gives a different id.
claims.source_hint: 'Git Internals - Git Objects' (object name is a hash over type, size and content); git-hash-object documentation

claims.text: A commit cannot be modified in place. Commands that appear to edit history write new commits with new ids; the replaced commit stays in the repository, no longer named by any branch, until Git clears out objects nothing points to any more.
claims.source_hint: git-gc documentation, DESCRIPTION (prunes unreachable objects after a grace period); git-commit --amend description ('creates a new commit object')

claims.text: Setting GIT_AUTHOR_NAME, GIT_AUTHOR_EMAIL, GIT_COMMITTER_NAME, GIT_COMMITTER_EMAIL, GIT_AUTHOR_DATE and GIT_COMMITTER_DATE fixes the author and committer lines of a commit, so the same sequence of changes produces the same commit ids on every machine.
claims.source_hint: git documentation, ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES, 'Committing' section; examples/don-hang at stage-0: git-playground/build-history.sh lines 13-24

claims.text: `git commit` writes into the `.git` folder of the local repository; `git push` is the command that sends your commits to another repository, so committing works with no connection.
claims.source_hint: git-commit documentation, DESCRIPTION; contrast git-push documentation, DESCRIPTION (the command that updates a remote)

claims.text: `git add -A` copies every change in the whole working tree into the staging area, and `git commit --message <msg>` writes the snapshot with that message without opening an editor.
claims.source_hint: git-add documentation, -A/--all; git-commit documentation, -m/--message

claims.text: Opinion: run `git status` and `git log --oneline --graph` before any other Git command in a repository, because together they state where you are standing and what is not yet saved.

claims.text: Git compresses stored objects and computes differences on demand, so 'a commit is a snapshot' describes what a commit means, not the bytes Git keeps on disk.

claims.text: `git show --stat <commit>` prints the commit followed by a list of the files it changed with counts of changed lines.
claims.source_hint: git-show documentation, DESCRIPTION; git-diff documentation, --stat

claims.text: A commit stores an author line and a committer line: the author is who wrote the change, the committer is who recorded it into the repository; they are usually the same person. HEAD names the commit currently checked out.
